title: Abram’s Call and the Egyptian Detour
summary: God calls Abram from Haran with promises of nation, land, and blessing for all families; Abram obeys and worships, then falters in Egypt.
historicalContext: Genesis 12 opens a new era. The scattering at Babel and the line of Shem lead to Terah’s household in Ur of the Chaldees, a wealthy Mesopotamian city devoted to the moon god, and then to Haran in the north, where the family halted (11:31). Joshua 24:2 remembers that Abram’s forebears “served other gods.” Probably early in the second millennium before Christ, Abram crossed into a Canaan of walled towns such as Shechem and Luz, later Bethel, whose people worshiped local deities and whose fields depended on seasonal rain. Pastoral clans moved between these towns, pitching tents on the outskirts and grazing flocks in the hill country and the Negeb. Egypt, watered by the Nile, served as a refuge for herdsmen from Asia in years of drought, and Egyptian paintings and texts depict such visitors arriving with families and animals. Abram enters this world as a wealthy but landless sojourner.
literaryContext: The chapter is the hinge between the history of the nations in chapters 1–11 and the story of the patriarchs. After a long pattern of sin and judgment ending at Babel, God speaks a word of blessing to one man for the sake of every family on earth. The chapter then falls into two contrasting halves. In verses 1–9 God speaks and appears, Abram is silent and obedient, and altars mark his route through Shechem and Bethel toward the Negeb. In verses 10–20 God neither speaks nor appears until the turning point in verse 17; human voices fill the scene, and Abram acts from fear and calculation. The Egyptian episode anticipates Israel’s later history: descent in famine, danger in Pharaoh’s land, plagues on Pharaoh’s house, and departure with wealth. Similar wife-sister episodes in 20:1–18 and 26:6–11 show that this weakness was neither isolated nor quickly overcome.
themes: God’s call and the obedience of faith
Blessing for all the families of the earth
The promised seed and the promised land
Worship as public witness among the nations
Fear, deception, and the failure of human schemes
God’s faithfulness that preserves His promise

outline.title: The Call and the Promise of Blessing
outline.summary: God commands Abram to leave his homeland and promises him a nation, a name, divine protection, and blessing for every family on earth.

outline.title: Departure from Haran
outline.summary: At seventy-five Abram obeys, taking Sarai, Lot, his household, and his possessions into Canaan.

outline.title: Altars in the Land
outline.summary: In Canaan the LORD appears and promises the land to Abram’s seed; Abram builds altars at Shechem and near Bethel and moves toward the south.

outline.title: Famine and a Fearful Plan
outline.summary: A severe famine drives Abram to Egypt, where he asks Sarai to call herself his sister to protect his life.

outline.title: Sarai Taken into Pharaoh’s House
outline.summary: Abram’s fears come true: Sarai is taken to the palace, and Abram is enriched on her account.

outline.title: The LORD Intervenes
outline.summary: God strikes Pharaoh’s house with plagues; Pharaoh rebukes Abram and sends him away with his wife and all he had.

verses.bibleText: Now the LORD had said unto Abram, Get thee out of thy country, and from thy kindred, and from thy father's house, unto a land that I will shew thee:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Now the LORD had said unto Abram” reaches back behind the family migration of 11:31. Stephen located the first summons in Mesopotamia, “before he dwelt in Charran” (Acts 7:2), and Genesis itself later recalls that the LORD brought Abram “out of Ur of the Chaldees” (15:7). The KJV’s pluperfect suits that history: the word that set Terah’s household moving had come first to Abram, and now, with the long halt at Haran behind him, it presses him onward. After eleven chapters in which human ambition repeatedly ended in judgment, the narrative turns on a sentence in which God alone takes the initiative. The God who called light out of darkness now calls one man out of a world that had gathered at Babel to make a name for itself.

The command moves inward in three circles: country, kindred, father’s house. Each is smaller and dearer than the last. Leaving a region is one thing; walking away from the clan that supplied protection, inheritance, and religious identity is far harder, and Joshua 24:2 remembers that Terah’s household “served other gods.” Abram is asked to stake his security, his name, and his future on the word of the One who calls him, with nothing in hand except that word.

The destination is held back: “unto a land that I will shew thee.” The verb is the causative of “see,” and the chapter will answer it when the LORD “appeared” to Abram in Canaan (v. 7). Abram knew the general direction, for the family had already set out toward Canaan, yet he could not know what the land would mean, where he would camp, or how long he would wait. Hebrews 11:8 puts it plainly: he “went out, not knowing whither he went.” Faith in this chapter is obedience to a Person whose character is trusted before the map is complete.

The same shape returns at Moriah, where Abram again hears “Get thee” and is again sent to a place God will name (22:2). Both moments ask him to release what he holds most dear. In this call the church hears its own summons. Jesus spoke of leaving house, brethren, and lands for His sake and the gospel’s (Mark 10:29-30), and the last book of Scripture calls God’s people out of Babylon (Revelation 18:4). The God who calls also goes with the one He calls.

wordNotes.term: לֶךְ־לְךָ (lekh-lekha) — get thee out
wordNotes.explanation: The imperative of halakh, “go,” is followed by a preposition carrying the pronoun, literally “go, for yourself.” The idiom stresses a decisive separation of the subject from his surroundings; it should not be stretched into a promise of self-discovery. The same rare construction returns in 22:2, binding Abram’s first and last great tests together. The verb halakh becomes the key word of the opening scene: God says “go,” and Abram “departed” (v. 4).

wordNotes.term: מוֹלַדְתְּךָ (moladtekha) — thy kindred
wordNotes.explanation: Related to the verb for bearing or begetting, the noun can denote a birthplace or the relatives among whom one was born. Standing between “country” and “father’s house,” it names the wider clan of Abram’s birth. Abraham later sends his servant back to this kindred to find a bride for Isaac (24:4), showing that leaving did not mean despising his family, only refusing to let it govern the course of his life.

verses.bibleText: And I will make of thee a great nation, and I will bless thee, and make thy name great; and thou shalt be a blessing:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The command of verse 1 is met by four promises in verse 2, and each answers something Abram is asked to surrender. He leaves a land and a clan; God will make of him “a great nation.” He forfeits the standing of his father’s house; God will “make thy name great.” The weight of the first promise falls on a couple without a child. Genesis has just reported, with unusual bluntness, “Sarai was barren; she had no child” (11:30). Every clause of verse 2 therefore depends on what God alone can do, and Abram’s whole story will turn on that dependence.

“I will bless thee” gathers up the blessing first spoken over humanity at creation (1:28) and renewed to Noah after the flood (9:1). In Genesis, blessing includes fruitfulness, prosperity, and protection, yet it reaches further. Paul treats the blessing given to Abram as including righteousness reckoned to faith (Galatians 3:8-9; Romans 4:3), so that material and spiritual good are held together under one promise.

“Make thy name great” sets Abram over against the builders of Babel, who said, “let us make us a name” (11:4). They sought renown by storming heaven; Abram receives it by following God. Their names are lost, while his is honored across the centuries by multitudes who look to him as father of the faithful. The same promise later comes to David (2 Samuel 7:9), and it reaches its height in Christ, who humbled Himself and was given “a name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:9).

The verse closes with a charge that carries the force of a promise: “and thou shalt be a blessing.” God does not intend Abram to be a reservoir that only collects. The favor resting on him is meant to pass through him to others, a purpose verse 3 will widen to every family on earth. Election here is a calling to serve, and the greatness promised is the greatness of usefulness in God’s hand.

wordNotes.term: גּוֹי גָּדוֹל (goy gadol) — a great nation
wordNotes.explanation: Goy usually names a people with land and political shape, and in Genesis 10 it describes the nations descended from Noah. God promises that Abram’s line will become such a nation among the nations, settled in a territory and ordered as a people. The word anticipates Israel at Sinai, called “an holy nation” (Exodus 19:6), and finally the people of God drawn from every nation and described in the same terms (1 Peter 2:9).

wordNotes.term: וֶהְיֵה בְּרָכָה (veheyeh berakhah) — and thou shalt be a blessing
wordNotes.explanation: The Hebrew verb is an imperative, “and be a blessing,” following the first imperative “go.” In this construction the second command states the result that follows from obeying the first: if Abram goes, a blessing he will be. The Greek Old Testament and the KJV render it as a future, which captures the certainty of the outcome. Blessing is both Abram’s gift and his vocation.

verses.bibleText: And I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee: and in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Verse 3 widens the promise in two directions. First, God binds His own dealings with the nations to their dealings with Abram: “I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee.” To take Abram’s side is to stand on God’s side. The phrasing is deliberately uneven. Those who bless are plural; the one who curses is singular, and the Hebrew uses a lighter verb for that person’s contempt and a weightier one for God’s response. God expects many to bless and few to despise, and His intention leans toward blessing. The promise is tested within this very chapter, when Pharaoh’s house suffers for taking Sarai (v. 17), and Balaam later learns that he cannot curse a people God has blessed (Numbers 24:9).

The last clause is the summit of the call: “in thee shall all families of the earth be blessed.” “Families” recalls the table of nations in chapter 10, where the clans of Noah’s sons spread over the earth before being scattered from Babel. The nations judged at Babel are not abandoned; Abram is chosen so that they may be reached. The word for “earth” here is ’adamah, the ground cursed because of Adam’s sin (3:17). Through one man the curse came; through the promised line of another the blessing will reach the same ground and the families who live on it.

The promise is not fulfilled by Abram in isolation. Later repetitions specify that the nations will be blessed “in thy seed” (22:18; 26:4; 28:14), and the New Testament names that Seed. Peter told the crowd in the temple that God had raised up His Servant Jesus and sent Him first to them to bless them, in fulfillment of this covenant (Acts 3:25-26). Paul calls the verse the gospel preached beforehand to Abraham, because God foresaw that He would justify the Gentiles through faith (Galatians 3:8). The first promise of 3:15 spoke of a Seed who would crush the serpent; here the same hope takes the shape of blessing for every people.

The verse sets the agenda for the rest of Scripture. Israel’s calling to be a light to the Gentiles (Isaiah 49:6), the commission to make disciples of all nations (Matthew 28:19), and the closing vision of a redeemed multitude “of all nations, and kindreds, and people, and tongues” (Revelation 7:9) all unfold from this sentence. Whoever belongs to Christ by faith is counted Abraham’s seed and an heir of the promise (Galatians 3:29). From its first announcement the blessing was meant for the world.

wordNotes.term: וְנִבְרְכוּ בְךָ (venivrekhu vekha) — in thee shall … be blessed
wordNotes.explanation: The verb is a Niphal form of barakh, a stem that can be passive (“be blessed”) or reflexive (“bless themselves”). The passive reading is well grounded: the Greek Old Testament renders it passively, and both Peter and Paul quote the promise in that sense. Even a reflexive sense would leave Abram as the means through whom the nations find blessing. The preposition can mean “in” or “through,” presenting Abram and his seed as God’s chosen instrument.

wordNotes.term: מְקַלֶּלְךָ אָאֹר (meqallelkha ’a’or) — him that curseth thee I will curse
wordNotes.explanation: Two different verbs stand behind the English “curse.” The first, from qalal, means to belittle, despise, or treat with contempt. The second, ’arar, is the solemn word of judicial curse used over the serpent and the ground (3:14, 17). Contempt for God’s chosen instrument meets a heavier sentence from God, while the singular form suggests such cases will be the exception.

verses.bibleText: So Abram departed, as the LORD had spoken unto him; and Lot went with him: and Abram was seventy and five years old when he departed out of Haran.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“So Abram departed, as the LORD had spoken unto him.” The narrator answers the command with the same verb: God said “go,” and Abram went. No speech of Abram is recorded, no bargaining, no request for terms. The phrase “as the LORD had spoken” recalls the obedience of Noah, who did “according unto all that the LORD commanded him” (7:5). In both men faith shows itself in ready action. Hebrews 11:8 draws the link explicitly: “By faith Abraham, when he was called to go out … obeyed.” Abram’s obedience grows out of trust; he goes because he believes the One who has promised.

“And Lot went with him.” Lot, the son of Haran who had died in Ur, had come north under Terah (11:31). Now he chooses to go on with his uncle. The New Testament remembers him as “just Lot” (2 Peter 2:7), and his readiness to share the journey reflects some measure of faith. His presence also raises a question the following chapters will settle: is this nephew to be the heir? Lot’s name appears twice in two verses, a hint that his story with Abram is far from finished.

Abram was “seventy and five years old when he departed out of Haran.” The age marks a turning point and starts a clock, for twenty-five years will pass before Isaac is born (21:5). Stephen says the move from Haran came after Terah’s death (Acts 7:4). That harmonizes with Genesis if 11:26 names Abram first for his importance rather than his birth order, just as Shem heads the list of Noah’s sons. A man who had spent three quarters of a century in Mesopotamia now begins life as a sojourner, an old beginner in the school of faith.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּלֶךְ (vayyelekh) — so … departed
wordNotes.explanation: The narrative form of halakh, “to go,” deliberately mirrors the command lekh in verse 1. This exact match between command and response is the narrator’s way of portraying faith without commentary. The same verb later describes walking before God as a manner of life (17:1; 24:40), so Abram’s journey becomes a picture of the believer’s daily walk.

wordNotes.term: כַּאֲשֶׁר דִּבֶּר אֵלָיו יְהוָה (ka’asher dibber ’elayw YHWH) — as the LORD had spoken unto him
wordNotes.explanation: This compliance formula presents Abram’s departure as obedience to revelation, more than a family migration. Closely related wording marks Israel’s faithful completion of the tabernacle (Exodus 39:43). Strikingly, the same words later describe God’s side of the relationship, when the LORD did unto Sarah “as he had spoken” (21:1). The servant acts as God has spoken, and God in turn keeps His word.

verses.bibleText: And Abram took Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother's son, and all their substance that they had gathered, and the souls that they had gotten in Haran; and they went forth to go into the land of Canaan; and into the land of Canaan they came.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Verse 5 slows down to list what went with Abram: “Sarai his wife, and Lot his brother’s son, and all their substance that they had gathered, and the souls that they had gotten in Haran.” The wording echoes 11:31, where Terah’s company “went forth … to go into the land of Canaan.” That earlier journey stalled at Haran. This one is completed: “into the land of Canaan they came.” The difference lies in the word of God. What Terah began and left unfinished, Abram brings to its goal because he travels at God’s call.

“All their substance” shows that Abram was already a man of means, with flocks, herds, and goods accumulated during the years in Haran. Wealth neither prevented his obedience nor became his security. He carried it as a steward who had placed his whole household under God’s direction. Scripture never treats possessions as evil in themselves; the danger lies in trusting them (Psalm 62:10; 1 Timothy 6:17). Abram’s later generosity toward Lot (13:8-9) and his refusal of Sodom’s spoil (14:22-23) show riches held with an open hand.

“The souls that they had gotten” uses nephesh in its ordinary sense of living persons. These were people attached to Abram’s household, servants and dependents from whom the 318 trained men of 14:14 would come. Since Abram and Sarai had no children, the phrase cannot mean offspring. At least some of these people had come to share Abram’s faith, for God later commends him for commanding “his household after him” to keep the way of the LORD (18:19). The man called to bless the nations began by bringing those nearest him into the knowledge of the true God.

The route from Haran to Canaan ran some four hundred miles through Syria. Genesis passes over its hardships in a single clause, because what matters is arrival in the place God had chosen.

wordNotes.term: הַנֶּפֶשׁ (hannefesh) — the souls
wordNotes.explanation: Nephesh here means persons, living human beings, as when Scripture counts “all the souls” of Jacob’s house who came into Egypt (46:27). The word describes the whole living person and not an immortal part separable from the body, in keeping with 2:7, where man “became a living soul.” Modern versions rightly render it “people” or “persons.”

wordNotes.term: רְכוּשׁ (rekhush) — substance
wordNotes.explanation: The noun denotes movable property, especially livestock and goods acquired over time, and here it is paired with its related verb, “gathered.” It recurs when Lot and Abram must separate and when the eastern kings carry off Sodom’s goods (13:6; 14:16), where property becomes a source of strife and peril. God later promises that Abram’s descendants will leave Egypt “with great substance” (15:14).

verses.bibleText: And Abram passed through the land unto the place of Sichem, unto the plain of Moreh. And the Canaanite was then in the land.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abram passed through the land unto the place of Sichem, unto the plain of Moreh.” A caravan from the north would have entered Canaan through the hills of Galilee and crossed the valley of Jezreel before climbing into the central highlands. Shechem lay in the pass between Mount Ebal and Mount Gerizim, near the geographic heart of the land, and was already a fortified town. Its place in Israel’s later story is large: Jacob camped and bought ground there (33:18-19), Joseph’s bones were laid to rest there (Joshua 24:32), and Joshua gathered the tribes there to renew the covenant (Joshua 24:1, 25). Abram’s first stop marks a spot where his descendants will one day pledge themselves to the God he worshiped.

“The plain of Moreh” is better rendered “the oak” or “terebinth of Moreh,” a great tree that served as a landmark. Moreh means “teacher” or “one who instructs,” and such trees were often linked with oracles and local cults. Abram adopts none of the rites of the place. He waits for the LORD, and the next verse records that the LORD came to him there. A site associated with human instruction becomes the place where God teaches His servant.

“And the Canaanite was then in the land.” Here “then” carries the sense of “already”: the land God had promised was not empty. It was settled, organized, and defended by peoples with their own cities and gods. Abram arrives as a foreigner without title to a single field. Whatever the promise meant, it would not be fulfilled by simple occupation. It would require faith that God would give in His own time what Abram could not take. Hebrews says he “sojourned in the land of promise, as in a strange country, dwelling in tabernacles” (Hebrews 11:9). The remark also prepares for 15:16, where God explains that the iniquity of the Amorites was not yet full. The long delay was itself an act of patience toward the Canaanites, who would see Abram’s altars and hear of his God.

wordNotes.term: אֵלוֹן מוֹרֶה (’elon moreh) — the plain of Moreh
wordNotes.explanation: ’Elon denotes a large tree, probably an oak or terebinth; the KJV’s “plain” follows an older interpretation. Moreh, a participle from the verb “to teach,” suggests “the teacher’s oak.” The same landmark is placed near Ebal and Gerizim in Deuteronomy, and the great tree at Shechem reappears when Jacob buries his household’s idols (35:4) and when Joshua sets up a stone of witness (Joshua 24:26).

wordNotes.term: וְהַכְּנַעֲנִי אָז בָּאָרֶץ (vehakkena‘ani ’az ba’arets) — and the Canaanite was then in the land
wordNotes.explanation: The adverb ’az, “then,” describes the circumstances of Abram’s arrival: the land was already inhabited. It need not imply that the Canaanites had gone by the time of writing, for they remained in the land in Moses’ day. The clause reminds the reader that the promise of verse 7 is given to an alien standing in someone else’s country.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD appeared unto Abram, and said, Unto thy seed will I give this land: and there builded he an altar unto the LORD, who appeared unto him.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the LORD appeared unto Abram.” At Haran God spoke; at Shechem He shows Himself. The verb is the passive of “see,” literally “was seen,” and it answers the promise of verse 1, “a land that I will shew thee.” The God who promised to show the land now shows Himself in it. Genesis does not describe the form of the appearance, yet the language belongs with later revelations in which the LORD comes to the patriarchs in perceptible ways (17:1; 18:1). Such appearances anticipate the One in whom God would make Himself fully known, the Word who became flesh and “dwelt among us” (John 1:14).

The message is brief, “Unto thy seed will I give this land,” only five words in Hebrew, and its brevity matches its boldness. It is spoken to a childless man of seventy-five, married to a barren wife, standing in a land held by walled Canaanite towns. Both elements, seed and land, seem out of reach. The promise also clarifies what verse 1 left open: the land is Canaan, and it is for Abram’s own offspring. Lot is not named. Stephen observed that God gave Abram no inheritance there, “not so much as to set his foot on,” yet promised it to him and his seed while he had no child (Acts 7:5). Abram’s faith must hold together a gift guaranteed and a gift deferred.

“Seed” runs through Genesis from 3:15 onward. It can mean a whole posterity or a single descendant, and Paul notes that the promises were spoken “to Abraham and his seed,” finding their focus in Christ (Galatians 3:16). The land promise itself widens in Scripture until Abraham is called “heir of the world” (Romans 4:13), and he is said to have looked for a city whose builder and maker is God (Hebrews 11:10). The hope of the patriarchs reaches its goal in the new earth God will give His people at the resurrection.

Abram answers with worship: “there builded he an altar unto the LORD, who appeared unto him.” The altar is the first claim he stakes in Canaan, and it claims the land for God before any field is Abram’s. An altar implies sacrifice, and sacrifice confessed sin and looked ahead in faith to the atonement God would provide (Hebrews 9:22). Among the shrines of the Canaanites, Abram’s altar announced that the LORD of heaven and earth was the true owner of this ground.

wordNotes.term: וַיֵּרָא (vayyera’) — appeared
wordNotes.explanation: The Niphal of ra’ah, “to see,” means “let himself be seen” or “appeared.” It echoes ’ar’ekka, “I will shew thee,” in verse 1, so the land God promised to show becomes the land in which He shows Himself. The same form introduces later revelations to Abram, Isaac, and Jacob, marking moments when God draws near in a perceptible way.

wordNotes.term: לְזַרְעֲךָ (lezar‘akha) — unto thy seed
wordNotes.explanation: Zera‘ is a collective noun that can denote many descendants or a single offspring, as when Eve calls Seth “another seed.” The Greek Old Testament renders it sperma, the word Paul draws on when he reads the promise as reaching its fulfillment in one Seed, Christ. Both senses stand together: a people descends from Abram, and through the one Seed the promise reaches its goal.

verses.bibleText: And he removed from thence unto a mountain on the east of Beth-el, and pitched his tent, having Beth-el on the west, and Hai on the east: and there he builded an altar unto the LORD, and called upon the name of the LORD.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
From Shechem Abram moved some twenty miles south “unto a mountain on the east of Beth-el,” pitching his tent on the high ground with Bethel to the west and Hai, or Ai, to the east. The town was still called Luz in Abram’s day (28:19); Moses uses the name it later bore, which means “house of God.” Jacob would give that name after his dream of the ladder, yet in this verse Abram already makes the place a house of God by worshiping there. Bethel later became a center of corruption when Jeroboam set up a golden calf in it (1 Kings 12:28-29). The town’s history runs from patriarchal worship to apostasy, a warning that sacred places do not preserve faith by themselves.

The verse sets two acts side by side: “pitched his tent” and “builded an altar.” The tent was temporary and would be struck when the flocks moved on. The altar remained. Abram’s life is pictured in those two structures: a pilgrim who held loosely to his dwelling and firmly to his God. Wherever he camped, worship was the fixed point.

He “called upon the name of the LORD.” The phrase first appears in 4:26, when worship began to be offered in Seth’s line, and it signifies public, spoken worship, prayer and praise addressed to God by His revealed name. Abram led a large household, so these gatherings would have been seen and heard by servants and neighbors alike. In a land given to the worship of Baal and other local deities, his altars bore witness to the Creator.

Centuries later Joel promised that “whosoever shall call on the name of the LORD shall be delivered” (Joel 2:32), and Paul applies those words to faith in Christ for Jew and Gentile without distinction (Romans 10:13). The worship Abram offered on a ridge in Canaan anticipates the call the gospel now carries to every nation.

wordNotes.term: וַיִּקְרָא בְּשֵׁם יְהוָה (vayyiqra’ beshem YHWH) — and called upon the name of the LORD
wordNotes.explanation: The expression means to invoke God by His personal name in worship, combining prayer, praise, and confession. It links Abram with the line of Seth and recurs at Bethel and Beersheba. The “name” stands for God’s revealed character; to call upon it is to rely on who He has shown Himself to be.

wordNotes.term: אָהֳלֹה (’oholoh) — his tent
wordNotes.explanation: The tent was the dwelling of the pastoral sojourner, movable and impermanent. Hebrews reads Abraham’s tents as a confession that he sought a lasting city prepared by God. Paul uses the same image for the mortal body, an earthly tent that will give way to a building from God at the resurrection.

verses.bibleText: And Abram journeyed, going on still toward the south.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Abram journeyed, going on still toward the south.” The Hebrew pictures a series of stages, breaking camp and moving on, as the household followed pasture and water toward the Negeb, the dry region south of the hill country where Beersheba would later become a center of patriarchal life. The highlands were already occupied by Canaanite towns and their fields, while the open grazing lands of the south offered room for large flocks.

The verse closes the first half of the chapter on a note of movement. Abram has received the land by promise, yet he lives in it as a traveler. The verse also prepares for what follows. The Negeb lies along the road to Egypt, and its scant rainfall made it the first region to feel a drought. Abram’s southward drift brings him to the edge of the land just as famine strikes. Genesis records no word from God directing this stage, and verses 10–20 will show what happens when Abram acts without seeking counsel.

wordNotes.term: הָלוֹךְ וְנָסוֹעַ הַנֶּגְבָּה (halokh venaso‘a hannegbah) — going on still toward the south
wordNotes.explanation: The doubled infinitives describe continuing action, moving by stages from one campsite to the next; nasa‘ originally meant pulling up tent pegs. Negev means the dry land and became the name of the southern region between the Judean hills and the wilderness, and therefore a word for “south.” Abraham and Isaac spent much of their lives there, around Gerar and Beersheba.

verses.bibleText: And there was a famine in the land: and Abram went down into Egypt to sojourn there; for the famine was grievous in the land.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And there was a famine in the land.” Abram has barely crossed Canaan when the land of promise fails to feed him. Canaan depended on autumn and winter rains, and when they failed the hills turned brown and the wells ran low. The famine was “grievous,” a word that stresses its weight. The narrator does not hide the irony: the land God promised seems unable to sustain the man to whom it was promised. Faith in the promise must now survive the experience of hunger inside the promise.

Egypt was the natural refuge. Its harvests depended on the annual flooding of the Nile rather than on local rain, and Egyptian records mention Asiatic herdsmen arriving at the frontier to keep their flocks alive. A tomb painting at Beni Hasan from roughly the patriarchal period shows a company of Semitic travelers with families and animals entering Egypt. Abram’s journey fits that world. Later Isaac faced a similar famine and was told not to go down to Egypt (26:1-2), and Jacob went only after God assured him, “fear not to go down into Egypt” (46:3). Abram receives no such word, and he does not appear to seek one.

Genesis neither commends nor explicitly condemns the move, but it registers a change in Abram’s posture. In verses 1–9 he followed the LORD’s word and built altars; here no altar is mentioned, no prayer, no calling upon the name. Abram went “to sojourn there,” intending a temporary stay, yet the decision placed him outside the land and among strangers. Throughout Scripture Egypt becomes a symbol of leaning on visible resources instead of on God (Isaiah 31:1; Jeremiah 2:18). The famine was a test meant to teach that even in Canaan bread comes from the LORD. Jesus met His own hunger test in the wilderness and answered that man lives “by every word that proceedeth out of the mouth of God” (Matthew 4:4).

wordNotes.term: כָבֵד הָרָעָב (khaved hara‘av) — the famine was grievous
wordNotes.explanation: Kaved means heavy or weighty and can describe burdens, honor, or severity. Here it marks a famine of crushing weight. The same root describes Abram in 13:2 as “very rich,” literally “very heavy” with possessions, an ironic pairing: he goes down to Egypt under the weight of hunger and comes back weighed down with wealth.

wordNotes.term: לָגוּר (lagur) — to sojourn
wordNotes.explanation: The verb gur describes residing as a resident alien, living among a people not one’s own without the rights of a native. The related noun ger names the stranger whom Israel was commanded to protect, because Israel too had been a stranger in Egypt. Abram’s sojourn there foreshadows that of his descendants.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, when he was come near to enter into Egypt, that he said unto Sarai his wife, Behold now, I know that thou art a fair woman to look upon:

commentary.detailedExplanation:
As the border approached, Abram turned to Sarai with words that sound like a compliment and work as a plan: “Behold now, I know that thou art a fair woman to look upon.” Sarai was about sixty-five years old (compare 12:4 with 17:17), yet in an age when life spans still exceeded a century she was in the middle of life; she lived to 127 (23:1). The Egyptians themselves noticed her beauty (v. 14). Genesis presents it as a plain fact.

Sarai’s beauty is no fault. The trouble lies in the conclusion Abram draws from it. “Behold now” introduces a request; he has been thinking ahead and has already settled on a strategy. What began as concern for his life has become reasoning without reference to God. The man who heard “I will bless them that bless thee, and curse him that curseth thee” now plans as though his safety rested on his own shrewdness. Fear reshapes perception: he looks at his wife and sees a danger to himself.

The Abram who obeyed without a word in verse 4 now speaks at length, and each sentence is driven by anxiety. Faith and fear can live side by side in the same believer, and the bright opening of this chapter did not shield Abram from its darker second half.

wordNotes.term: יְפַת־מַרְאֶה (yefat-mar’eh) — fair to look upon
wordNotes.explanation: The phrase joins yafeh, “beautiful,” with mar’eh, “appearance,” and is used of Rachel and, in the masculine, of Joseph. In each story outward beauty draws attention that brings danger or temptation, and in each God works through the situation. Scripture values beauty as a gift of the Creator while warning that it cannot secure what only God can give.

verses.bibleText: Therefore it shall come to pass, when the Egyptians shall see thee, that they shall say, This is his wife: and they will kill me, but they will save thee alive.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Abram’s prediction is exact: “when the Egyptians shall see thee, … they will say, This is his wife: and they will kill me, but they will save thee alive.” He imagines a powerful man who desires Sarai and removes the husband who stands in the way. The fear was not baseless. Scripture later records exactly this crime when David arranged Uriah’s death in order to keep Bathsheba (2 Samuel 11:14-17), and foreigners had few protections in the ancient world. Abram knew how powerful men could behave.

Yet the reasoning shows how far his focus has narrowed. He foresees his own death and Sarai’s survival, but he does not weigh what her “survival” would mean: life in another man’s house, separated from her husband and from the promise. His fear is for himself. Nor does he reckon with the God who had just appeared to him at Shechem and promised the land to his seed.

If Abram were killed before he had a child, the promise would seem to fail, and Abram may have felt he must protect God’s plan by his own devices. That instinct, helping God by setting aside what God has said, will surface again in chapter 16 with Hagar. The promise never needed human deceit to keep it alive. It needed trust in the One who made it, and who had said, “I will curse him that curseth thee.”

wordNotes.term: וְהָרְגוּ אֹתִי וְאֹתָךְ יְחַיּוּ (veharegu ’oti ve’otakh yechayyu) — they will kill me, but they will save thee alive
wordNotes.explanation: The sentence sets two objects in contrast, “me” and “thee,” with the verbs “kill” and “keep alive” (the Piel of chayah). The arrangement exposes Abram’s self-concern. The same pairing of killing and keeping alive returns when a later Pharaoh orders Israel’s sons killed and daughters kept alive.

verses.bibleText: Say, I pray thee, thou art my sister: that it may be well with me for thy sake; and my soul shall live because of thee.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Say, I pray thee, thou art my sister.” The request was a half-truth. Sarai was the daughter of Abram’s father by another mother (20:12), so she was in fact his half-sister. The purpose of the statement, however, was to conceal the marriage, and words framed to mislead are a lie whatever technical accuracy they contain. Chapter 20 reveals that this was a standing arrangement the couple had agreed upon when they first left home (20:13). The plan was no impulse at the border; it was a policy shaped by fear long before the danger appeared.

Abram gives two reasons: “that it may be well with me for thy sake; and my soul shall live because of thee.” The repeated “me” and “my” reveal the center of his concern. He may have hoped that as Sarai’s brother he could negotiate, delay, or decline any proposal, since a brother had a voice in such matters (compare 24:50-51; 34:11-12). On human terms the plan made sense. In practice it exposed Sarai to the very danger it was meant to avoid and placed the mother of the promised seed in jeopardy.

“My soul shall live” uses nephesh for Abram’s life itself; he means “that I may stay alive.” Nothing here suggests a conscious part of Abram that would survive his death. The nephesh is the living person whose life he fears to lose, and Genesis uses the word this way throughout. Death would end that life until God restores it in the resurrection.

Scripture tells this failure honestly, and the honesty belongs to its message. The father of the faithful was not chosen for a flawless record, and his descendants could never boast in him. A believer may obey God boldly in one crisis and give way to fear in the next. Jesus spoke to that weakness when He told His disciples, “Fear ye not therefore, ye are of more value than many sparrows” (Matthew 10:31). God’s care made Abram’s deception unnecessary.

wordNotes.term: אֲחֹתִי (’achoti) — my sister
wordNotes.explanation: ’Achot can mean a full or half-sister and, more broadly, a female relative. Abraham later explains that Sarah was “the daughter of my father, but not the daughter of my mother.” Marriage to a half-sister was afterward forbidden in Israel’s law, but it had not yet been prohibited in patriarchal times. Using a true kinship term to hide the more important truth of marriage made the statement deceptive.

wordNotes.term: וְחָיְתָה נַפְשִׁי (vechayetah nafshi) — and my soul shall live
wordNotes.explanation: Nafshi, “my soul,” is an idiom for “I myself” or “my life.” The clause means simply that Abram will stay alive, and it parallels “that it may be well with me.” Lot uses the same expression when pleading to flee to Zoar. Nephesh here, as at creation, is the living self, not an immortal entity.

verses.bibleText: And it came to pass, that, when Abram was come into Egypt, the Egyptians beheld the woman that she was very fair.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And it came to pass, that, when Abram was come into Egypt, the Egyptians beheld the woman that she was very fair.” Abram’s prediction is fulfilled almost word for word. What he feared would be seen was seen. Egyptian art and stories reflect a taste at court for women from abroad, and a woman from the north with a stately bearing would have drawn notice.

The verse is brief, and its restraint is purposeful. The scheme seems to be working: Abram is alive, and no one has threatened him. Yet the narrative is moving steadily toward an outcome he had not imagined. Sarai is simply “the woman” here, seen by the Egyptians only as a beauty, never as a wife. The deception has stripped her of the one identity that would have protected her, and Abram’s lie has made her available. A truthful answer might have spared her what follows.

wordNotes.term: יָפָה הִוא מְאֹד (yafah hi’ me’od) — she was very fair
wordNotes.explanation: The narrator adds “very” to Abram’s earlier description, confirming his estimate and heightening the danger. Me’od is the same intensifier used when God saw all He had made and it was “very good.” Beauty is a good gift of the Creator, yet in a fallen world it can be looked upon with covetous eyes.

verses.bibleText: The princes also of Pharaoh saw her, and commended her before Pharaoh: and the woman was taken into Pharaoh's house.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“The princes also of Pharaoh saw her, and commended her before Pharaoh: and the woman was taken into Pharaoh’s house.” The officials of the court, always alert to what might please the king, praised her to their master. The verb rendered “commended” is the word for praise that fills the Psalms, where it is directed to God. Here it serves the appetites of a royal court.

“Pharaoh” was originally an Egyptian expression meaning “great house,” a term for the palace that came to designate the king himself. Genesis does not give this ruler a personal name. What matters to the narrative is the office: the most powerful man in the region has taken the wife of the man through whom God promised to bless the world.

“The woman was taken.” The passive verb leaves Sarai without a voice. She does not speak in the entire episode, and Abram, so far as the text records, raises no protest. Entry into the royal household would ordinarily have been the first stage toward marriage, with a period of preparation before a woman was brought to the king. The mother of the promised line now lives in a palace where she does not belong, and the word of 12:7 hangs on God alone. Abram has kept his life and lost his wife, and only the LORD can recover what his scheme has surrendered.

wordNotes.term: וַתֻּקַּח הָאִשָּׁה (vattuqqach ha’ishshah) — and the woman was taken
wordNotes.explanation: The verb is a passive form of laqach, “to take,” which is often used for taking a wife. Here it describes Sarai being removed from her husband by the power of a king. Pharaoh will later use the active form of the same verb when he admits, “so I might have taken her to me to wife” (v. 19).

wordNotes.term: פַּרְעֹה (par‘oh) — Pharaoh
wordNotes.explanation: The title comes from an Egyptian expression meaning “great house,” first the royal palace and then the king who lived in it. It appears here for the first time in Scripture and dominates the stories of Joseph and the exodus. The Pharaohs of Genesis and Exodus are identified by office, not by personal name.

verses.bibleText: And he entreated Abram well for her sake: and he had sheep, and oxen, and he asses, and menservants, and maidservants, and she asses, and camels.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And he entreated Abram well for her sake.” Abram’s words in verse 13 return to him: he had asked Sarai to lie “that it may be well with me for thy sake,” and now the king deals well with him for her sake. On its own terms the scheme has succeeded. The gifts are lavish: sheep, oxen, male and female donkeys, menservants and maidservants, and camels. Such presents were customary when a ruler took a woman into his household, something like a bride-price paid to her family. Abram accepts them, and in accepting them he receives payment for his wife.

The list is an inventory of wealth in the ancient Near East. Camels were less common than other animals at the time, but they were known, and their mention fits a royal gift meant to impress. The Egyptian handmaid Hagar, who appears in chapter 16, may have joined Sarai’s service during this stay; if so, one consequence of the episode would trouble the household for generations.

The irony is heavy. God had promised, “I will bless thee,” and Abram now grows rich, yet this wealth comes by way of deceit, and it cannot satisfy because Sarai is gone. Genesis distinguishes prosperity granted by God from prosperity obtained by compromise. “The blessing of the LORD, it maketh rich, and he addeth no sorrow with it” (Proverbs 10:22); Abram’s new herds came with sorrow attached. Jesus asked what a man would profit if he gained the whole world and lost his own soul (Mark 8:36). Standing among his flocks without his wife, Abram had gained possessions at a price no herd could repay.

wordNotes.term: הֵיטִיב (heitiv) — entreated well
wordNotes.explanation: The Hiphil of yatav, “to be good,” means to do good to someone or treat him favorably. It picks up Abram’s own word in verse 13, “that it may be well (yitav) with me,” showing that his wish has come true in an unexpected and painful way. Jacob later clings to God’s promise, “I will surely do thee good,” using the same verb; lasting good comes from God’s hand.

wordNotes.term: גְּמַלִּים (gemallim) — camels
wordNotes.explanation: The camel was known in the early second millennium, though not yet widely used, and ancient figurines and remains attest its presence. Its place at the end of the list marks the gift as exceptional. Camels later carry Abraham’s servant to Mesopotamia in search of a bride for Isaac and bear the Ishmaelite traders who buy Joseph.

verses.bibleText: And the LORD plagued Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai Abram's wife.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And the LORD plagued Pharaoh and his house with great plagues because of Sarai Abram’s wife.” For the first time since verse 8 the LORD is named, and He acts decisively. Abram has been silent before God; Sarai has been silent altogether; God Himself has seemed absent. Now the divine name stands at the center of the episode, and the whole situation turns. The narrator also restores Sarai’s true identity: she is “Abram’s wife.” What the lie concealed, the LORD exposes.

The plagues are not described. They were evidently such that Pharaoh connected them with Sarai, perhaps through her own disclosure or by some divine warning like the dream given to Abimelech (20:3). Whatever their form, they guarded Sarai and compelled her release. The promise of verse 3 is fulfilled at once and in an unexpected way. Pharaoh had acted without knowing Sarai was married, yet taking another man’s wife was a real wrong, and judgment fell on the house that held her. The psalmist recalls this protection: God “suffered no man to do them wrong: yea, he reproved kings for their sakes; saying, Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm” (Psalm 105:14-15).

Grace stands out sharply here. God intervenes for a man who has failed Him. Abram did not deserve rescue; he had placed his wife in danger and profited by it. Yet the LORD remained faithful to His promise and to Sarai, who was essential to it. “If we believe not, yet he abideth faithful: he cannot deny himself” (2 Timothy 2:13). Such faithfulness gives no license for presumption. To sin deliberately while counting on God to rescue us is to tempt Him, as Jesus said when urged to throw Himself from the temple (Matthew 4:7).

The plagues also foreshadow the exodus. Abram’s descendants would one day go down to Egypt in famine, suffer under a Pharaoh, and be released after God struck Egypt with plagues. The God who rescued Sarai from Pharaoh’s house would rescue Israel from Pharaoh’s land.

wordNotes.term: וַיְנַגַּע … נְגָעִים גְּדֹלִים (vaynagga‘ … nega‘im gedolim) — plagued … with great plagues
wordNotes.explanation: The verb naga‘ in the Piel means to strike or afflict, and the related noun nega‘ denotes a blow, often in the form of disease. The same noun names the final stroke on Egypt at the exodus and the skin afflictions examined by the priests. Pairing verb and noun from the same root stresses the severity of the judgment.

wordNotes.term: עַל־דְּבַר שָׂרַי (‘al-devar Saray) — because of Sarai
wordNotes.explanation: Literally “on account of the matter of Sarai.” The same expression recurs when God closes the wombs of Abimelech’s household “because of Sarah.” In both stories God takes up the cause of a woman whom her husband had failed to protect, showing that His care for the promise includes care for the person through whom it would come.

verses.bibleText: And Pharaoh called Abram, and said, What is this that thou hast done unto me? why didst thou not tell me that she was thy wife?

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Pharaoh called Abram, and said, What is this that thou hast done unto me?” The roles are reversed. The pagan king speaks with moral clarity, and the man of God stands rebuked. Pharaoh’s question echoes the LORD’s question to Eve in the garden, “What is this that thou hast done?” (3:13). Abram is called to account as Adam’s children have always been, and this time the voice of rebuke comes from an unbeliever.

The king presses, “why didst thou not tell me that she was thy wife?” His words imply that he would never have taken Sarai had he known the truth. Whatever else may be said of Pharaoh, he recognized the sanctity of marriage and was offended at being placed where he might violate it. Abram had assumed that foreigners had no fear of God, as he would later say of Gerar (20:11). He was wrong, and fear proved a poorer guide than truth.

Abram makes no reply. In chapter 20 he will offer explanations; here he has none. His silence before the king is a picture of every believer whose conduct has given the world cause to blame. Paul warned that the name of God can be blasphemed among the Gentiles because of those who claim to know Him (Romans 2:24), and Peter urged believers to keep their conduct honest among unbelievers, so that slander might be answered by good works (1 Peter 2:12). Abram had been called to be a blessing to the nations; in Egypt, through fear and deception, he had become the occasion of their suffering.

wordNotes.term: מַה־זֹּאת עָשִׂיתָ לִּי (mah-zo’t ‘asita li) — What is this that thou hast done unto me?
wordNotes.explanation: This form of accusing question recurs in Genesis wherever wrongdoing is brought to light: God to Eve, Abimelech to Abraham and later to Isaac, and Jacob to Laban. It is less a request for information than a summons to face what has been done.

verses.bibleText: Why saidst thou, She is my sister? so I might have taken her to me to wife: now therefore behold thy wife, take her, and go thy way.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Pharaoh presses his complaint: “Why saidst thou, She is my sister? so I might have taken her to me to wife.” The KJV’s “I might have taken” renders a Hebrew construction that can also mean “so that I took her.” Pharaoh describes his intention and the steps already taken toward marriage, and he lays the blame on the lie that led him there. The text does not say that the marriage was consummated, and the parallel account in chapter 20 shows God acting to prevent exactly that (20:6). The plagues came in time to guard Sarai, and the mother of the promised seed was preserved.

“Now therefore behold thy wife, take her, and go thy way.” The king’s words are short and sharp. There is no further discussion; he wants Abram and his troubles out of the country. Yet he neither punishes him nor reclaims the gifts. The plagues have taught him to fear the God who stands behind this man, and he shows Abram more restraint than Abram had expected from him.

The scene humbles Abram before the very people he was meant to bless. Still the promise stands, and God’s purpose moves forward. Sarai is restored, the couple is reunited, and the way back to Canaan opens. Grace does not erase the shame of the episode, but it overrules its consequences, and Abram leaves with a lesson he would have to learn again in Gerar.

wordNotes.term: וָאֶקַּח אֹתָהּ לִי לְאִשָּׁה (va’eqqach ’otah li le’ishshah) — so I might have taken her to me to wife
wordNotes.explanation: The consecutive verb can express result: “so that I took her as my wife.” Laqach le’ishshah, “take as wife,” is the standard idiom for entering marriage. Pharaoh admits that he moved toward marriage, yet he blames Abram’s deception for it. The account does not describe consummation, and God’s swift judgment protected Sarai.

verses.bibleText: And Pharaoh commanded his men concerning him: and they sent him away, and his wife, and all that he had.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And Pharaoh commanded his men concerning him: and they sent him away, and his wife, and all that he had.” Pharaoh assigns men to escort Abram to the border. The arrangement is both courtesy and expulsion: Abram is protected, but he is no longer welcome. He leaves with Sarai and with all his possessions, the royal gifts included. The verse closes the episode with a list that mirrors its opening. Abram went down because of famine; now he goes back laden with wealth and with his wife restored to him.

The verb “sent away” carries further echoes. It is used when God sent Adam out of the garden (3:23), and it becomes the key verb of the exodus, where the LORD demands, “Let my people go,” literally “send away my people” (Exodus 5:1). Abram’s departure from Egypt after plagues on Pharaoh’s house previews what God will do for his descendants. They too will go down to Egypt in famine, be enriched by the Egyptians as they leave (Exodus 12:35-36), and return to the land of promise. Abram’s story becomes Israel’s story in miniature, and the God who rescued the father will rescue the children.

The chapter ends with the promise intact despite Abram’s failure. Chapter 13 shows him returning to Bethel, to the altar he had built at the beginning, and calling again on the name of the LORD (13:3-4). The way back from failure runs through worship. Abram’s calling rested on grace from its first word, and that same grace brings him home.

wordNotes.term: וַיְשַׁלְּחוּ (vayshallechu) — and they sent him away
wordNotes.explanation: The Piel of shalach means to send off, release, or dismiss. It describes God sending Adam out of Eden and Pharaoh releasing Israel after the plagues. The echo ties Abram’s departure from Egypt both to humanity’s loss and to Israel’s coming deliverance.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: What would it take for you to leave what is familiar on the strength of God’s word alone?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God calls Abram by grace to receive and carry a blessing meant for all nations, and He keeps that promise even when Abram’s faith gives way to fear.
discussionQuestions: Why does God’s command in verse 1 move from country to kindred to father’s house?
How do the promises of verses 2–3 answer the ambitions of the builders of Babel?
What do Abram’s altars at Shechem and Bethel teach about worship and witness?
What led Abram from the faith of verses 1–9 to the fear of verses 10–13?
How does God’s intervention in Egypt show that the promise rests on grace rather than on Abram’s performance?
commonMisunderstandings: Abram’s call was not a reward for exceptional goodness; it came by God’s initiative to a family that had served other gods.
Being chosen did not make Abram the final destination of the blessing; he was chosen to carry it to all nations.
God’s rescue in Egypt does not approve Abram’s deception; Pharaoh’s rebuke exposes the wrong.
The wealth Abram gained in Egypt is not evidence that God endorsed his conduct.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the call and the failure together: the God who speaks the promise is also the God who preserves it, so that the hope of the nations rests on His faithfulness.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Hear Christ’s call to follow Him, let worship of the true God mark every place you pitch your tent, and trust Him in the famine as fully as at the altar.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: The blessing promised to Abram is the gospel of righteousness by faith, offered to every nation through Christ, Abraham’s Seed.
flow: After Babel, humanity stood scattered under judgment and in need of blessing.
God called Abram and promised that through him all families of the earth would be blessed.
That promise is fulfilled in Jesus Christ, the Seed of Abraham.
All who believe in Christ are counted Abraham’s children and heirs of the promise.
Like Abram, believers answer God’s call with trusting obedience.
simpleIllustrations: A deed to an inheritance has value before the property is seen; Abram set out holding God’s promise while the land still lay ahead.
A spring that fills only its own basin grows stagnant, but one that runs into a stream waters a whole valley; God meant Abram’s blessing to flow outward.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you answer God’s call by trusting Christ, the Seed through whom the blessing of Abraham comes to you?
cautions: Do not present Abram as a flawless hero; his failure in Egypt shows that grace sustains the promise.
Do not reduce the blessing to material prosperity; the New Testament centers it in righteousness by faith.
Do not turn verse 3 into a political program; the New Testament locates its fulfillment in Christ and all who belong to Him.

reflectionQuestions: What familiar security might God be asking me to release so that I can follow Him?
Do I treat the blessings I have received as meant to flow through me to others?
Where in my daily life is there a visible altar, a place of worship that those around me can see?
When pressure comes, do I seek God’s counsel or reach first for my own schemes?
How have I seen God remain faithful to me even when I was unfaithful to Him?
